overview.prompt: A client asks why the provider performs a rectal exam to check for prostate cancer. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Most tumors arise in the urethra next to the bladder
Most tumors arise in the seminal vesicles behind the bladder
Most tumors arise in the transition zone around the urethra
Most tumors arise in the peripheral zone near the rectum

overview.rationale: Most adenocarcinomas arise commonly in the peripheral zone near the rectum, which can make a lesion palpable on DRE. BPH usually develops in the transition/periurethral zone.

overview.prompt: A client with BPH asks whether his enlarged prostate means he has cancer. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “BPH can turn into prostate cancer over time.”
“BPH is a different disease, though both can coexist.”
“An enlarged prostate can confirm cancer is there.”
“BPH can be thought of as early prostate cancer.”

overview.rationale: BPH is not the same disease as prostate cancer and can coexist with it; an enlarged prostate alone does not establish cancer.

overview.prompt: A client with metastatic prostate cancer asks where it most commonly spreads through the blood. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The spine, pelvis, ribs, and hips
The brain, as the usual first site
The skin and subcutaneous tissue
The thyroid and salivary glands

overview.rationale: Bloodborne spread commonly involves the axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs, hips), with lung/liver and less commonly brain involvement. Skin and thyroid are not typical sites, and the brain is not the usual first site.

overview.prompt: A client is told his cancer is now “castration-resistant” and asks if he can stop his leuprolide. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It grows despite castrate testosterone; ADT continues
The cancer has been cured by the castration therapy
Hormone signaling is irrelevant, so ADT is stopped
Testosterone has risen too high for the ADT to work

overview.rationale: Castration-resistant cancer progresses despite castrate testosterone levels; it does not mean androgen signaling is irrelevant or that all hormonal treatments must stop.

manifestations.prompt: A client with metastatic prostate cancer reports new severe back pain and leg weakness. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait until bladder control is lost
Give an analgesic and reassess tomorrow
Encourage walking to relieve the pain
Arrange immediate emergency assessment

manifestations.rationale: New severe back pain with leg weakness suggests possible spinal cord compression and needs immediate emergency assessment; do not wait for paralysis or incontinence.

manifestations.prompt: A client with no urinary complaints has a newly elevated PSA and asks how cancer could be present without symptoms. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Cancer usually causes a weak urinary stream.”
“Early prostate cancer is often asymptomatic.”
“Early cancer usually shows up as bone pain.”
“Without symptoms, cancer is usually ruled out.”

manifestations.rationale: Early prostate cancer is often asymptomatic and may be detected through PSA-based evaluation rather than symptoms. Absence of symptoms does not rule it out, and urinary or bone symptoms are not required.

manifestations.prompt: A client reports noticing blood in his semen. How should the nurse document this finding?

options.text: Hematochezia
Anejaculation
Hematospermia
Gross hematuria

manifestations.rationale: Hematospermia means blood in semen; hematuria means blood in urine, hematochezia is blood in stool, and anejaculation is absence of ejaculate. Hematospermia warrants assessment but is not specific to cancer.

risk.prompt: A client asks what the strongest common risk factor for prostate cancer is. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Increasing age
High caffeine use
Past vasectomy
Frequent cycling

risk.rationale: Increasing age is the strongest common risk factor, with disease much more frequent after 50. The other options are not listed risk factors.

risk.prompt: A nurse is planning community prostate cancer education. Which group has higher US incidence and mortality?

options.text: Non-Hispanic White men
Hispanic/Latino American men
Asian/Pacific Islander men
Black/African American men

risk.rationale: Black/African American men have higher US incidence and mortality; this supports timely risk discussion and access without assuming individual outcomes.

risk.prompt: A healthy client in his mid-70s with no symptoms asks for a routine PSA screening test. What does the current USPSTF recommendation state?

options.text: It recommends PSA tests on alternate years for him
It recommends screening by DRE alone at his age
It advises against screening in this age group
It recommends yearly PSA screening for older men

risk.rationale: USPSTF recommends against routine PSA-based screening at age 70 or older; this does not prohibit investigating symptoms. Yearly or every-other-year PSA and DRE-only screening are not its recommendation for this age group.

risk.prompt: A client’s brother was diagnosed with prostate cancer at a fairly young age. The client asks if this affects him. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Just a father’s diagnosis affects your risk.”
“That family history raises your own risk.”
“Family history has no effect on your risk.”
“Your risk is exactly three times higher.”

risk.rationale: A father, brother, or son with prostate cancer increases risk, particularly with younger diagnosis or multiple relatives. The ‘doubles to triples’ figure is an approximate association, not a fixed personal multiplier.

diagnostics.prompt: A client with a recent urinary tract infection has an elevated PSA. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: Infection may raise PSA; context must be assessed
PSA may be unaffected by infection or procedures
An elevated PSA may confirm cancer on its own
A biopsy may be required automatically today

diagnostics.rationale: Elevated PSA can reflect BPH, prostatitis/infection, recent procedures, and other temporary influences; confirm and assess context before automatic biopsy.

diagnostics.prompt: A client’s biopsy shows Gleason 4+3=7, and a friend’s showed 3+4=7. The client asks if they mean the same thing. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Yes, the same total gives the same grade group.”
“No, yours has more of the higher-grade pattern.”
“No, your friend’s has more aggressive cancer.”
“Gleason scores aren’t used to describe grade.”

diagnostics.rationale: Primary/secondary patterns matter: 4+3=7 is Grade Group 3 and 3+4=7 is Grade Group 2, so a 4+3 tumor is not equivalent to 3+4 despite the same total. Higher groups generally indicate more aggressive disease.

diagnostics.prompt: On the evening after a prostate biopsy, which client report needs urgent follow-up?

options.text: Slight blood in the stool once
Light blood in the urine
Fever with shaking chills
Mild soreness in the rectum

diagnostics.rationale: After biopsy, report fever/chills, inability to void, severe pain, or heavy/persistent bleeding urgently; expected minor bleeding is explained beforehand.

diagnostics.prompt: A client with a high PSA says, “My rectal exam was normal, so I don’t need an MRI.” What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “A normal DRE excludes prostate cancer.”
“A normal DRE doesn’t rule out cancer.”
“DRE is more accurate than PSA testing.”
“DRE lets the doctor see the prostate.”

diagnostics.rationale: A normal DRE does not rule out cancer; DRE is palpation, not direct visual inspection, and is an adjunct.

medical.prompt: A client with low-risk prostate cancer chooses active surveillance. How does this differ from watchful waiting?

options.text: It means no monitoring until symptoms appear
It means starting ADT right away for life
It is the same program under a different name
Structured monitoring that keeps a cure option

medical.rationale: Active surveillance is structured monitoring with PSA, MRI, and repeat biopsy as indicated, preserving a curative option; watchful waiting is symptom-directed observation.

medical.prompt: A client asks how LDR brachytherapy differs from HDR brachytherapy. Which response is accurate?

options.text: LDR uses a temporary source; HDR leaves seeds
LDR leaves permanent seeds; HDR’s source is removed
Both are forms of external-beam radiation therapy
Both leave permanent seeds in the prostate gland

medical.rationale: LDR commonly leaves permanent seeds after image-guided implantation; HDR uses a temporary source that is removed.

medical.prompt: A client’s cancer has become castration-resistant, and a new agent is added. What happens to his ADT?

options.text: The ADT backbone continues
ADT is given just during pain
ADT is replaced by vitamin E
ADT is stopped going forward

medical.rationale: Continue the appropriate ADT backbone in castration-resistant disease; additional therapies are added according to criteria.

medications.prompt: A client with bone metastases is starting leuprolide and is also prescribed a short antiandrogen course. He asks why. What is the best explanation?

options.text: To prevent irritation at the leuprolide injection site
To cover the early testosterone surge from leuprolide
To raise testosterone levels and strengthen his bones
To replace leuprolide after the very first injection

medications.rationale: An agonist’s early surge can worsen bone pain/obstruction; selected patients receive short antiandrogen coverage.

medications.prompt: Which ADT agents avoid the initial testosterone surge seen with GnRH agonists?

options.text: Alpha-blocker drugs such as tamsulosin
GnRH agonists such as leuprolide or goserelin
5-alpha reductase inhibitors such as finasteride
GnRH antagonists such as degarelix or relugolix

medications.rationale: GnRH antagonists such as degarelix/relugolix avoid the initial testosterone surge; leuprolide and goserelin are agonists with a surge.

medications.prompt: A client is starting abiraterone. Which accompanying plan should the nurse expect?

options.text: A daily potassium supplement with no lab checks
Monthly hearing tests and dilated eye examinations
A prescribed steroid plus BP, potassium, liver checks
Stopping other ADT before the first abiraterone dose

medications.rationale: Abiraterone commonly requires a prescribed steroid and BP/potassium/liver review. Unmonitored potassium, stopping ADT, or hearing/eye tests are not part of its standard plan.

medications.prompt: A client taking finasteride for BPH is having a PSA drawn. Why should the nurse make sure the clinician knows about this medicine?

options.text: Finasteride lowers PSA
Finasteride raises PSA
Finasteride treats the cancer
Finasteride doesn’t change PSA

medications.rationale: Finasteride treats selected BPH and lowers PSA, so the interpreting clinician needs that history; it is not definitive cancer treatment.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client receiving external-beam radiation asks if he must stay away from his grandchildren. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “Avoid close contact with children until it ends.”
“Your urine will be radioactive for about a week.”
“Use separate dishes for the whole treatment course.”
“This type of treatment doesn’t make you radioactive.”

nonpharmacological.rationale: External-beam treatment does not make the patient radioactive; seed and radioligand precautions are different.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client with permanent LDR seeds finds a seed in the urine strainer. What should he do?

options.text: Avoid bare fingers; follow radiation-safety steps
Pick it up by hand and flush it down the toilet
Ignore it, since a single loose seed is harmless
Throw it out with the household trash right away

nonpharmacological.rationale: If a seed passes, do not handle it with bare fingers; use the provided instructions/equipment, keep it away from others, and contact radiation safety.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client scheduled for nerve-sparing prostatectomy says, “At least I know my erections won’t change.” What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “Nerve-sparing surgery doesn’t guarantee erectile function.”
“Erectile changes only happen after radiation.”
“Erections will improve beyond baseline after surgery.”
“That’s right; nerve-sparing always preserves erections.”

nonpharmacological.rationale: Nerve-sparing surgery does not guarantee erectile preservation; sexual rehabilitation and referral should be discussed.

adverse-effects.prompt: After a traditional monopolar TURP, a client becomes confused and nauseated with a low sodium. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Absorbed hypotonic irrigant causing hyponatremia
Bladder spasms from the inflated catheter balloon
Expected anesthesia effects that need no action
Opioid withdrawal in the hours after surgery

adverse-effects.rationale: Systemic absorption of hypotonic irrigant during monopolar TURP can cause dilutional hyponatremia/fluid overload with confusion; escalate promptly.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client asks what sexual changes to expect after radical prostatectomy. Which change is common?

options.text: Guaranteed preserved erections
Increased ejaculate volume
Retrograde ejaculation into bladder
Dry orgasm and infertility

adverse-effects.rationale: Radical surgery commonly causes dry orgasm/anejaculation and infertility from loss of prostate/seminal-vesicle contributions. Retrograde ejaculation is more typical after TURP, and erections are not guaranteed.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client is starting ADT. Which adverse effects should the nurse teach him to expect or report? Select all that apply.

options.text: Frequent hot flashes
Gain in muscle mass
Reduced breast tissue
Increased libido
Gradual bone loss

adverse-effects.rationale: ADT causes hot flashes, reduced libido/ED, gynecomastia, fatigue, mood changes, muscle loss, weight gain, and bone loss/fracture risk. Libido decreases, muscle is lost rather than gained, and breast tissue may enlarge (gynecomastia) rather than shrink.

nutrition.prompt: A client asks if vitamin E supplements are safe for preventing prostate cancer. What did the SELECT trial find?

options.text: Benefit when combined with selenium
No meaningful effect on cancer risk
Clear protection against prostate cancer
Higher cancer risk in the treated group

nutrition.rationale: SELECT found increased risk with the studied vitamin E supplementation, so it should not be used for prevention. It did not show protection, and selenium is not a proven substitute.

nutrition.prompt: A postoperative client’s catheter has had no drainage for some time and he has lower abdominal pain. A family member suggests he drink more water. What does the nurse know?

options.text: Oral hydration is the first-line treatment here
Extra water will flush the blockage out quickly
He should drink a large volume over the next hour
Fluids won’t clear a blocked tube; assess patency

nutrition.rationale: Drinking water cannot fix a blocked catheter; absent drainage with pain suggests obstruction needing assessment and escalation.

nutrition.prompt: Which nutrition assessment is most important for a client on long-term ADT?

options.text: Calcium/vitamin D intake and bone/muscle health
Daily vitamin E intake to prevent cancer growth
High-dose selenium intake for tumor control
Sugar intake as the main cause of hot flashes

nutrition.rationale: During ADT, assess calcium/vitamin D intake, bone/fracture risk, and muscle preservation, using prescribed bone therapy when indicated. Vitamin E and selenium are not proven preventive treatments.

assessment.prompt: A client reports a weak stream and feeling of incomplete emptying. What should the nurse avoid advising?

options.text: Checking for suprapubic distention
Measuring urine amount and color
Straining to empty the bladder
Assessment for possible obstruction

assessment.rationale: Assess possible obstruction instead of advising straining; Valsalva to empty a poorly draining bladder is not routine.

assessment.prompt: A client has known bone metastases. Which findings are most important for the nurse to assess at each visit?

options.text: Hair loss, skin color, and nail bed changes
Hearing, vision, and overall dental health
Taste changes and appetite as the main focus
New back pain, leg strength, bladder changes

assessment.rationale: Assess new or changing bone/back pain, gait, leg strength/sensation, and new bowel/bladder dysfunction to detect cord compression or fracture early. The other findings do not screen for these emergencies.

diagnoses.prompt: A client receiving chemotherapy for prostate cancer develops thrombocytopenia. Which nursing diagnosis is most directly supported?

options.text: Risk for impaired swallowing
Disturbed sensory perception
Risk for bleeding
Risk for disuse syndrome

diagnoses.rationale: Thrombocytopenia means the platelet count is low, increasing bleeding risk. The diagnoses section links bleeding risk to cytopenias and cancer treatment. No swallowing, sensory, or immobility findings support the other options.

diagnoses.prompt: A client has new back pain with leg weakness. How should the nurse handle this problem?

options.text: Add a routine mobility diagnosis
Document it as chronic cancer pain
Plan teaching at the next visit
Seek urgent medical assessment

diagnoses.rationale: Suspected cord compression, sepsis, and obstructed drainage require urgent medical assessment, not only a routine nursing diagnosis. Deferring teaching or labeling it chronic pain delays time-critical treatment.

priorities.prompt: During ordered CBI after TURP, catheter outflow stops and the client has painful bladder distention. After checking for kinks, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Increase the irrigation rate to clear clots
Keep the inflow running and recheck later
Stop irrigation inflow and escalate promptly
Give oral fluids to increase urine flow

priorities.rationale: Stop irrigation inflow if outflow is obstructed and promptly obtain urologic review; do not keep filling an obstructed bladder.

priorities.prompt: After radical prostatectomy, a client’s urinary catheter falls out. What is the nurse’s priority action?

options.text: Reinsert a new catheter at the bedside now
Teach the client to reinsert it on his own
Wait to see whether he can void on his own
Obtain prompt urology advice; don’t reinsert

priorities.rationale: Catheter dislodgement needs prompt urology advice to protect the anastomosis; do not independently remove/reinsert or blindly manipulate the catheter.

plan.prompt: A client on ADT has had a stable PSA for several months but new hip pain. How should the nurse evaluate cancer control?

options.text: Stable PSA alone isn’t enough; assess symptoms
Monitoring can stop since the PSA is stable
Hip pain is unrelated as long as PSA is stable
A stable PSA proves the cancer is controlled

plan.rationale: A stable PSA alone is not enough to declare every treatment successful; clinical trends and symptoms are reviewed.

plan.prompt: How should continence and erection outcomes be evaluated after prostate cancer treatment?

options.text: By comparing him to one fixed recovery timeline
By promising a full recovery of function
By ignoring them while the cancer is controlled
By client-chosen goals, not a promised recovery

plan.rationale: Use patient-selected outcomes and teach-back rather than promising identical continence or erection recovery for everyone. Fixed timelines and ignoring function do not reflect individualized care.

interventions.prompt: A client is receiving continuous bladder irrigation. How should the nurse determine his true urine output?

options.text: Add the irrigant volume to the total drainage
Record the irrigant volume as urine output
Record total drainage as the urine output
Subtract the irrigant volume from total drainage

interventions.rationale: True urine output equals drainage minus irrigant (for example, 3,800 mL drained − 3,000 mL instilled = 800 mL). Recording total drainage overestimates output, and adding or substituting the irrigant volume is incorrect.

interventions.prompt: A client after TURP reports painful bladder spasms. Before giving the prescribed oxybutynin, what should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess catheter patency
Remove the indwelling catheter
Increase oral fluid intake
Irrigate with large volume

interventions.rationale: Assess patency before giving a prescribed antispasmodic, since obstruction can mimic spasm. Fluids, unordered large-volume irrigation, or removing the catheter are not appropriate first steps.

interventions.prompt: A client going home with a catheter asks when to empty the drainage bag. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Before it gets too full, such as half-full
Once a week on the same day each week
When urine begins to leak from the bag
When the bag is filled right to the top

interventions.rationale: Teach bag emptying before it becomes too full (often about half-full), with hand hygiene and securement. Waiting until full or leaking increases backflow and traction risk.

education.prompt: A client at home after prostate surgery calls about his catheter. Which report requires prompt contact with the team?

options.text: Light pink urine after walking
Large clots with no drainage
Small amount of leakage while walking
Mild urge feeling at the tip

education.rationale: Worsening bright-red bleeding, large clots, distention, no drainage, or catheter loss needs prompt contact; some light blood may be expected.

education.prompt: After radical prostatectomy, a client asks when to start pelvic-floor exercises. What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Immediately, while the urinary catheter is in place
Once incontinence has lasted longer than a year
Avoid them, since they would strain the incision
When the team advises, such as after catheter removal

education.rationale: Practice pelvic-floor technique when the surgical/PT team advises, often after catheter removal. Starting before advised or avoiding it entirely is not recommended.

evaluation.prompt: Two months after complete radical prostatectomy, which PSA result is expected?

options.text: A temporary PSA bounce
An unchanged PSA
An undetectable PSA
A slowly rising PSA

evaluation.rationale: PSA should become undetectable after complete radical prostatectomy; a slower fall and possible bounce occur after radiation.

evaluation.prompt: Which outcome best shows that radiation-safety teaching was effective?

options.text: He plans to throw passed seeds in the trash
He uses one standard interval for each therapy
He says external beams make him radioactive
He explains his own seed or radioligand plan

evaluation.rationale: Evaluation: the patient accurately explains the specific seed or radioligand instructions and has an achievable household plan. Applying one interval to every treatment or misunderstanding external-beam radiation shows teaching gaps.
